notes:
Patient has been under my care since 2018.

HEARING IMPAIRMENT:
Patient was diagnosed with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss in 2018 following a viral infection.
Left ear: profound hearing loss (91dB+). Right ear: severe hearing loss (71-90dB).
Patient uses bilateral behind-the-ear hearing aids but continues to have significant difficulty.
Despite hearing aids, patient requires repetition constantly, relies heavily on lip-reading, and cannot 
understand speech in any environment with background noise. Even in quiet settings with a familiar person,
patient cannot understand verbal communication without lip-reading.
Patient is unable to hear adequately to understand a familiar person in a quiet setting even with devices.
This is the case all or substantially all of the time.
Year impairment began: 2018. Expected to be permanent — No improvement expected.
The impairment has lasted for more than 12 months.

MENTAL FUNCTIONS:
Patient also has ADHD and Major Depressive Disorder diagnosed in 2016.
Takes medication (sertraline + atomoxetine) — moderately effective. Requires reminders to take medication.
Uses CBT and a daily schedule/planner as assistive tools.

Regarding independence: Patient has impaired capacity to live independently.
Receives support from family members and community-based health services.

Mental function ratings compared to peers:
- Adaptive functioning — performing everyday tasks: severe limitations
- Adaptive functioning — go into community: some limitations
- Attention — impulse control: severe limitations
- Concentration — focus on simple tasks: severe limitations
- Goal-setting — make and carry out plans: severe limitations
- Goal-setting — self-direct to begin tasks: severe limitations
- Judgment — understand consequences: some limitations
- Memory — remember simple instructions: some limitations
- Regulation of behaviour: severe limitations
- Regulation of emotions: severe limitations

Patient is unable to perform mental functions necessary for everyday life without inordinate time/effort,
all or substantially all of the time. Year began: 2016. No improvement expected. Lasted 12+ months.

CUMULATIVE EFFECT:
Patient has significant limitations in both hearing and mental functions. These limitations exist together
all or substantially all of the time. The cumulative effect is equivalent to a marked restriction.
Year cumulative limitations began: 2016.
Impairments are not expected to improve — permanent.

CERTIFICATION:
I have been this patient's physician since 2018 to present.
Medical information on file: Yes.
Practitioner type: Medical doctor

notes:

I am this child's pediatrician and have followed them since birth in 2017. They were diagnosed in 2019 with autism
spectrum disorder (level 3, requiring very substantial support) and intellectual disability.

Communication: the child is minimally verbal, with about 20 single words. They cannot make themselves understood by
anyone outside the family, even with their picture exchange system (PECS) and speech-generating device. This is the case
all or substantially all of the time. Speech has been impaired since the 2019 diagnosis, this has lasted more than
12 months, and it is not expected to improve. They attend speech-language therapy weekly.

Medication: risperidone for severe irritability and aggression. The parents give and supervise every dose.
It is mildly effective.

Other therapy: applied behaviour analysis 20 hours per week, occupational therapy, and visual schedules.

Independence: compared with other children of the same age, the child needs far more support.
They require one-to-one adult supervision at home at all times.
At school they have a full-time educational assistant and an individualized education plan.

Mental function ratings compared to peers:
- Adapting to change: severe limitations
- Expressing basic needs: severe limitations
- Awareness of danger (runs into traffic): severe limitations
- Regulation of behaviour: severe limitations
- Understanding verbal information: some limitations
- Basic hygiene and toileting: some limitations

Because of these limitations the child is unable, or takes an inordinate amount of time, to perform the mental functions
needed for everyday life, all or substantially all of the time. This began in 2019 and has lasted more than 12 months.
It is uncertain whether these mental functions will improve.

Medical records are on file. I have been the child's physician from 2017 to present.

notes:
Neurology follow-up - clinic note

S: 52-year-old with multiple sclerosis, diagnosed 2014, now secondary progressive. Reports worsening leg weakness and
fatigue. Numbness and poor coordination in both hands make buttons, zippers and shoelaces very difficult.

O: Spastic paraparesis, worse on the left. Walks with a four-wheeled walker. Walking 100 m takes about 2.5 minutes
with one rest break. Reduced fine motor dexterity in both hands.

Medications: ocrelizumab infusions every 6 months; baclofen 10 mg three times daily for spasticity.
Other therapy: physiotherapy weekly. Uses a button hook and elastic shoelaces for dressing.

A: Multiple sclerosis with significant limitations in walking and in dressing.
Walking: significantly limited since 2021, but walking does not take three times longer than for someone of the same age.
Dressing: significantly limited since 2022. The patient dresses without help, but needs about twice the normal time.
Neither limitation on its own is a marked restriction.
The walking and dressing limitations exist together all or substantially all of the time, and their cumulative effect
is equivalent to a marked restriction in one basic activity of daily living. The cumulative effect began in 2022.
All limitations have lasted more than 12 months and are not expected to improve.

P: Continue ocrelizumab and baclofen. Occupational therapy referral for home adaptations.

Patient under my care since 2016 to present. Records on file.

notes:
The patient is a 68-year-old who had a left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke in March 2023.
I have been their family physician since 2010.

Since the stroke they have expressive aphasia and dysarthria. They cannot make themselves understood by strangers, and
even family members understand only short phrases. A conversation takes more than three times as long as for someone
of the same age, because they must write words down or point to a picture board. This is the case all or substantially
all of the time. They attend speech-language therapy twice a week and use a tablet communication app.
No medication is taken for the speech impairment.

They also have oropharyngeal dysphagia from the stroke and need a pureed diet with thickened fluids. Weakness in the
right hand means they cannot cut food or open containers. They eat with a weighted spoon and a plate guard.
Each meal takes over an hour, more than three times longer than normal, all or substantially all of the time.
No medication is taken for the feeding impairment.

Both impairments began in 2023 and have lasted more than 12 months. With ongoing therapy, their speech-language
pathologist expects speech to improve by 2027. The feeding impairment is not expected to improve.

Medical records are on file. Under my care from 2010 to present.

notes:
Re: Disability Tax Credit - supporting medical information

I have followed this patient in my clinic since 2012. They have type 1 diabetes mellitus, diagnosed in 2009,
complicated by proliferative diabetic retinopathy diagnosed in 2016.

VISION
Despite panretinal laser photocoagulation and intravitreal anti-VEGF injections, vision has continued to deteriorate.
Best corrected visual acuity, measured on a Snellen chart at the most recent visit:
  Right eye: 20/400
  Left eye: 20/200
Visual field: 15 degrees in the right eye and 20 degrees in the left eye.
The patient meets the criteria for blindness in both eyes.
Vision has been impaired to this degree since 2019 and this has lasted more than 12 months.
Vision is not expected to improve.

LIFE-SUSTAINING THERAPY
Type 1 diabetes was diagnosed prior to 2021.
Insulin is delivered by an insulin pump, with continuous glucose monitoring.
Every day the patient checks blood glucose, counts carbohydrates and adjusts insulin doses, at least 4 times per day
(28 times per week).
Time spent on these activities averages 16 hours per week.
This therapy supports a vital function (regulation of blood glucose).
Insulin therapy has been required since 2009 and has lasted more than 12 months. It is lifelong and will not improve.

I have been this patient's physician from 2012 to present. Their medical records are on file in this clinic.
